To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a common pathway of chromosomal abnormalities is shared by HCCs from both HBV and non-B, non- C patients; 2) some of the chromosomal abnormalities are preferentially associated with HBV-induced carcinogenesis; 3) the chromosomal abnormalities of fibrolamellar HCCs are distinct from those of non-fibrolamellar HCCA.

the chromosomal abnormalities found in HCCs from patients with no detectable HBV or HCV infection are similar to those detected in HCCs of HBV-positive patients, but that some abnormalities are more frequently associated with viral infection.

a common chromosomal aberrations pattern was detected in non-B, non C and in HBV positive HCC, and that a distinct chromosomal abnormality patterns were observed in non-B, Non C and in HBv positive HCC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of chromosomal abnormalities associated either with the development or progression of primary liver cancer.
the identification of genetic alterations that are common or unique to HCCs of different etiology and to the rare fibrolamellar subtype of this cancer.
the identification of chromosomal alterations associated with HCC, with a focus on non-viral cases, in which the etiology is unknown and the prognosis is poor.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CGH analysis is a useful tool in the diagnosis and prognosis of primary liver cancer.
chromosomal aberrations in HCC are not related to HBV and HCV infection.
a common pathway of chromosomal alterations exists for all HCCs, but that a subset of these changes may be more frequently involved in virus-induced carcinogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CGH analysis of HCCs is a powerful method to identify the chromosomal regions that are frequently altered in this disease, and that it may help in the identification of genes involved in the etiopathogenesis of HCC.

chromosomal alterations in HCC may be divided into three groups: 1) those that are common to all HCCs, regardless of etiology; 2) those that are associated with a particular etiology; and 3) those that are specific to a particular subtype of the disease.
, in addition to the common pathway towards malignance, a subset of chromosomal alterations may be associated with the etiologies of HCC.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CGH analysis of primary HCC is a powerful tool in dissecting the complex molecular events leading to the development of liver cancer.
chromosomal abnormalities associated to HCC are not only dependent on the etiology of the disease, but also on the histologic subtype.
the CGH analysis of HCCs can provide valuable information for understanding the molecular pathogenesis of this disease.
